chunks: Rijal al-Kashshi: Hamduwayh, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Ibn Miskan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid who said:

I met al-Hasan ibn al-Hasan, and he said: Do we not have a right? Do we not have a sanctity? If you were to select from among us a single man, he would have been sufficient for you! I did not have an answer for him, so I met Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and informed him of what he had said to me. He said to me: Meet him and say to him: We came to you and said: Do you have what the rest do not have? You said: No, so we considered you truthful and you became deserving of that [status]. Then we came to the sons of your uncle and said: Do you have what the people do not have? They said: Yes, so we considered them truthful and they became deserving of that. He said: So I met him and said to him what he had said to me. Al-Hasan said to me: But we do have what the people do not have. I did not have anything [to reply], so I came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and informed him. He said to me: Meet him and say: Indeed, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says in His book: 'Bring me a book before this or traces of knowledge, if you are truthful.' So sit down for us so that we may ask you. He said: So I met him and argued against him with that. He said to me: Do you not have anything other than to humiliate us? If so-and-so [Ja'far] chose to be free [from revolt] and we were engaged [in revolt], then that is what takes away our right!

key_terms.بَنِي عَمِّكُمْ: Sons of your uncle (referring to the descendants of Husayn)

ai.seo_question: What argument did al-Hasan ibn al-Hasan use to claim the Imamate, and how did Imam al-Sadiq refute it using the Quran?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Rijal al-Kashi* illustrates the early theological dispute between the Hasanids and the Prophet's family regarding the nature of Imamate, specifically contrasting the claim of exclusive scholarly authority against the necessity of divine proof. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) employs the Quranic verse 46:4 to challenge the Hasanids' assertion of possessing unique knowledge (*atharat min 'ilm*) that distinguishes them from others, demanding tangible evidence rather than mere lineage. The narrative underscores the Shia position that true Imamate requires both spiritual authority and distinct, verifiable knowledge, critiquing the Hasanid reliance on the Prophet's scholarly dedication as insufficient for establishing their specific right.
